notes: Complete, consistent replacement using Token and Dispenser helpers, matching the reference apart from minor nits, with strong dispenser and table-driven parser tests including error cases.

Closely mirrors the reference with clean Token helpers plus Dispenser wrappers applied at every brace site; it adds thorough dispenser and parse tests, including error cases for an unclosed block and a quoted '{' after an address.
Mirrors the reference closely with clean Token methods on every structural check, and adds thorough tests: a dispenser test plus parse cases for nesting, heredoc and an unclosed-block error.

Complete and idiomatic Token-method approach covering all brace sites including ArgErr, addresses and the doImport anonymous-block check; tests cover dispenser NextBlock, backtick and heredoc braces, nested blocks and an unclosed-block error.

Covers all the structural sites the reference covers except the HasSuffix and quoted-{} nits; it mixes the helper with inline Quoted() checks, and good parser and dispenser tests include a nested block.

Near-complete coverage including the doImport anonymous-block check and removal of the redundant wasQuoted check, though the doImport switch and addresses inline the logic instead of reusing the helper; tests include a nested block and a NextBlock dispenser case.

Converts nearly every structural brace check to an unquoted-only helper, but misses the anonymous-block check in doImport and keeps a now-redundant wasQuoted guard; tests check both segment tokens and dispenser args.

Covers the dispenser, ArgErr, addresses and the parser brace checks with Token and Dispenser helpers, but adds redundant bounds checks (Token() already guards) and misses the doImport anonymous-block check; the tests verify both segment tokens and NextArg.

Fixes the reported case but misses the addresses() open-brace check and the doImport anonymous-block check, duplicates parser methods that shadow the Dispenser ones, and its tests only assert that no error occurs.

Misses the addresses() check, so a quoted '{' after a site address is still treated as a block opener, and it scatters duplicate helpers across files with parser methods shadowing Dispenser ones; the tests only assert that no error occurs.
Fixes the main parsing paths but misses ArgErr and the doImport anonymous-block check, and puts the Token methods oddly in dispenser.go; tests are adequate but parser-only.

Fixes the core block-parsing paths in the dispenser and parser, but leaves ArgErr and the doImport anonymous-block check comparing raw text, keeps a now-redundant wasQuoted check, and places the Token helpers oddly in dispenser.go; the tests cover only simple parse cases.

A single depth-based slug substitution covers both branch and regular page dirs, keeps intermediate segments and unnormalized case, and comes with the most thorough test (nested slugged section, non-section subdir, taxonomy and term).

Replaces path segments by section depth, which correctly covers nested sections, non-section intermediate directories, plain subdirectories, taxonomies, terms and unnormalized paths; the test covers these cases well.

Replaces slugged segments by depth in the unnormalized section base and prefix-rewrites container dirs, which preserves intermediate directories and case; the change is compact and correct, with a solid multilingual and taxonomy test.

Clean depth-indexed slug replacement on the section base plus a CutPrefix for regular pages handles nested gaps and unnormalized paths correctly; the test covers the main scenarios but not nested slugs or plain subdirectories.

Builds the section dir from the ancestor chain with slugs and prefix-rewrites regular page container dirs with a proper boundary check; it handles the issue, taxonomies and terms, but rebuilding from per-ancestor base names drops intermediate non-section directories (e.g. docs/a/b/_index.md whose parent section is /docs).

Builds the section dir from ancestor names or slugs and prefix-replaces it for regular pages, which works in the common cases, but rebuilding from per-section base names drops intermediate directories that are not sections.

The recursive slug dir with a 'changed' flag works for the issue and taxonomies and handles nested non-section dirs for regular pages, but concatenating parentDir plus the base name loses intermediate directories between non-adjacent sections, and the logic is somewhat convoluted.

The recursive slug-dir builder handles sections, taxonomies, terms, pages in plain subdirectories and DisablePathToLower, but once an ancestor has a slug it drops any non-section directories between nested sections (e.g. section /a/b/c with parent /a).

Rewrites regular page dirs only on an exact match with the section base, so pages in nested non-section dirs keep the original path; it also uses the lowercased Path(), which breaks disablePathToLower, and it fails a hidden test.

Applies the slug to a regular page only when its container dir equals the section base exactly, so pages in plain subdirectories are missed; it also builds segments from normalized Path(), ignoring DisablePathToLower, and fails one hidden test.

Returns a clean slice in declaration order, tracks the declaring module per config resource, and adds a defensive fix for slice aliasing. It still resolves parent/child overrides per config resource rather than per instance, as the reference does. Its fixture test locks in the over-broad override.

Fixes the reported root-module for_each case, but a parent import still overrides at ConfigResource level, so a child's import of a different instance is silently dropped; its unit test explicitly asserts that drop (the slice-aliasing fix on cfg.Path is a nice touch).

Keeps every same-module block by storing a map of slices, which fixes the reported for_each case. It still overrides child-module imports at the config-resource level, so a parent import of one instance silently drops the child's imports of other instances. Its unit test asserts that wrong behavior even though the count, for_each and module coverage is otherwise good.

Keeps a map of slices with nondeterministic Values() order and the same resource-level parent override that drops child imports of other instances; has the strongest tests (for_each, count, module) but they also codify that drop.

Uses the same map-of-slices approach as C1 and fixes the single-module case. It shares the same flaw: a parent block for one instance still silently discards the child's blocks for other instances (and other module instances). It adds only a minimal for_each plan test.
Same map-of-slices approach as C2 with the same nondeterministic ordering and resource-level override gap; its single context test covers only the basic repro.

A tidy slice plus claimedBy-map rewrite that fixes the reported for_each case. Overrides remain at config-resource granularity, so child imports for other instances are still dropped silently. It adds a single three-instance plan test.
Clean slice plus claimedBy-map approach that fixes the reported case, but it still silently discards child-module imports of other instances whenever a parent imports any instance of that resource.

The simplest version: a slice with a linear scan for parent overrides, which is quadratic but works for the reported case. It has the same per-resource rather than per-instance override flaw. Only a basic for_each test is added.

Simple slice with an O(n^2) linear scan for the parent-override check, which keeps the resource-level override that drops child imports of different instances; the test covers only the root-module repro.
Equivalent to C4 but keys the owners map by string address instead of using addrs.Map, which is less idiomatic. It shares the cross-module override gap. Its test does not check the planned action.
Returns a slice with an owner map keyed by stringified addresses (less idiomatic than addrs.Map) and has the same resource-level override gap; its single test does not check the planned action.

The post-consolidation rewrite works for all commands and the consolidation tests are thorough (runner shortcuts, browser options, multiple scenarios, conflicts, --once=false). Drawbacks: the flag is validated twice, the test harness duplicates the production call, and there is an unrelated stdlog_integration_test change.

Rewrites the consolidated config after the merge, so run, cloud run and archive all see the change, and it preserves exec/env/tags/options; however it does not stop lower-layer shortcuts (e.g. K6_ITERATIONS) from wiping script scenarios during the merge, it checks the flags twice, and it includes an unrelated stdlog proxy test edit.

Placing applyOnce inside getConsolidatedConfig covers every consumer, including archive, cloud and local-execution, and the consolidation tests cover env, script and file layers plus conflicts. Remaining gaps: lower-layer shortcuts can still wipe script scenarios before the merge, and execution-segment flags are not rejected.

Applies --once inside getConsolidatedConfig with proper exit codes and wires all three CLI config getters including local execution; it has thorough consolidation tests (env layer, browser options, startTime discarded), but script scenarios can still be wiped by lower-layer shortcuts during the merge.
It applies after DeriveScenariosFromShortcuts, so the archive and cloud path miss --once, and `cloud run --local-execution` never sets Once. It also includes an unrelated stdlog proxy test rewrite.

Applies --once only to the derived config after DeriveScenariosFromShortcuts, so archive and cloud run (which use consolidated options) ignore it; it also leaves stale shortcuts behind, never wires the flag into --local-execution, and adds an unrelated stdlog test change.
It pushes a CLI-only field into the public lib.Options struct and its Apply logic, and applies in deriveAndValidateConfig so archive and cloud runs ignore --once. The package suite fails.

Pollutes the public lib.Options with a CLI-only field and applies the transform only in deriveAndValidateConfig, so archive and cloud never see it; conflict errors also lack the InvalidConfig exit code.

It applies the rewrite to the consolidated options in test_load.go, so run, archive and cloud all get it, and the patch is small and focused. Gaps: an env-layer shortcut can still wipe script scenarios before the rewrite, execution-segment conflicts are not rejected, and the tests are thin unit tests.

Minimal, clean implementation applied to the consolidated options so the archive and cloud get it; it misses lower-layer shortcut handling, calls cmd.Flags() without a nil guard, and its tests are only unit-level.

The transform runs inside deriveAndValidateConfig, after the consolidated options have been captured. As a result, `k6 archive` and non-local `k6 cloud run` never see --once and would upload the full load, which matches the failed hidden tests and package suite.

Wiring is reasonable, including local execution, but the transform runs during derivation, so archive and cloud run upload untransformed consolidated options, and flag-conflict errors lack the InvalidConfig exit code.

Essentially the reference approach (unified wrap helper applied in the paren and unary paths, plus the Pretty fix), with comprehensive printer and evaluation tests; only StartPos and EndPos differ slightly from the reference.

Closely matches the reference: one helper wraps a bare NumberLiteral in a Wrapped unary-plus DurationExpr for both the paren and unary paths, and Pretty is updated to match. Positions use the literal start rather than the paren, and parser, printer and promqltest eval tests are thorough.

Uses a clean unified wrap helper and updates Pretty, and also unwraps through the new node in positive_duration_expr so `foo[(0s)]` still fails at parse time; the grammar touch is slightly beyond the issue but is justified and backed by thorough tests.

Same clean approach as the reference, plus Pretty, plus an unwrap that keeps parse-time validation for `(0s)`. That unwrap only sees through unary plus, so `-(5s)` still falls back to eval-time checking; test coverage is solid.

Wraps bare literals in a unary-plus DurationExpr in both the paren and unary paths and updates Pretty; the wrapper construction is duplicated instead of reusing the helper, and StartPos points at the literal rather than the paren, but the printer and eval tests are thorough.

Correct fix with Pretty updated and good tests, but the wrapping DurationExpr is built inline in applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr instead of reusing wrapNumberLiteral, and the old split branch logic is kept.

Fixes round-trip and preserves parse-time positive-duration errors, including for `-(5s)`, with good tests, but skips the Pretty update and places its helpers somewhat awkwardly at the end of the file.

Fixes the round-trip and keeps parse-time 'duration must be greater than 0' errors for `(0)` and `-(5s)` via an unwrap helper, with error tests. Pretty is not updated, `wrapDurationExpr` only wraps literals despite its name, and the helpers are tacked on at the end of the file.
Correctly wraps literals with paren-accurate positions that match the reference and uses a neat recursive call in the unary path, but omits the Pretty unary-plus change, so Pretty would print `(+5)`.

Round-trip is fixed. However, Pretty is not updated, so the new unary-plus node would pretty-print as `+5` and diverge from String(). Positions also differ between the paren path (paren positions) and the unary path (literal positions), and there are no eval tests.

Uses a unified wrap helper close to the reference, but guesses paren positions with literal Start-1/End+1 (wrong when whitespace is present), keeps a redundant Wrapped assignment, does not update Pretty, and has no printer test for `+(5)`.

Works for common inputs, but guesses paren positions as literal±1, which breaks with whitespace. It also redundantly re-sets Wrapped, leaves a stale comment, skips the Pretty update, and adds only minimal tests.

Well-designed ReturnValue sentinel: the context-carried value is cleared for nested executions, the boundary trap is added to the fork script, `try` passes returns through, and the tests are thorough; however, valued returns are lost at `template` boundaries and it rewrites `return x | f` rather than rejecting it, changing an existing regression test.

Clean panic sentinel with HasValue, nested-context isolation, try passthrough and a fork-script update; it also adds pipeline wrapping (`return x | f`) and silently discards value returns at template boundaries, both diverging from the reference.

Clean ErrReturn sentinel trapped at the execution and template boundaries, with `try` passthrough, a context-carried partial value, and correct bare-return output; it silently ignores pipeline commands after return and edits exec.go without updating the fork script, but has good tests and passes everything.

Uses a simple panic-based ErrReturn trapped at executeWithState and walkTemplate, re-panics through try, and carries the value via a context side channel; it works broadly with good tests, though it edits exec.go without a fork-script change and silently ignores values in non-partials.

The panic-based sentinel works anywhere, including in `{{ template }}` calls and through `try`, but has three weaknesses: a partial with any valued return yields nil when execution falls through, valued returns are swallowed at template boundaries, and exec.go is edited directly without updating the fork script (plus a dangling leftover comment).

Reasonable panic-based sentinel with try passthrough and boundary trapping, but it edits generated exec.go directly (errRecover and walkTemplate) without updating the fork script, leaves an orphan comment, and a partial with an unexecuted value return yields nil.

A return inside `{{ template }}` aborts the whole outer template because there is no boundary trap, partials containing any return discard output (a bare return gives nil), and `try` passthrough is missing; the pipeline-position error check is a nice match to the reference.

Adds the 'return must be last in pipeline' check, but has no template-boundary trapping, lets try swallow the return ExecError, keeps HasReturn so output is discarded (bare return gives nil), and its test asserts an ugly `%!s(<nil>)` result.

Routes return entirely through the normal 'error calling' error path with no executor changes, so `template` boundaries aren't respected, `try` swallows returns, and bare returns in partials give nil; it also leaves the dead keep/slices.Delete logic and a gofmt misalignment.

The return error is wrapped as a normal exec error and only caught at the top-level store, so `{{ return }}` inside a `{{ template }}` aborts the whole outer template. The kept HasReturn flag discards a partial's output whenever any return exists, even one that never runs.

It traps return at template boundaries via the ExecError wrapper, but a bare return in a partial yields nil instead of the output rendered so far; `try` passthrough is missing, arg-wrapping only applies when the next arg is an identifier, and ExecuteWithContextAndKey now leaks ReturnError to other callers.

Traps returns at template boundaries via the ExecError wrapper, but a bare return in a partial yields nil instead of the rendered output, and ExecuteWithContextAndKey now leaks the sentinel as an error to callers.
